While delayed clamping for 1–3 minutes is linked to increased blood volume and iron stores, an hour-long delay is not part of current medical consensus.

**Step 3: Conclusion**
Based on the evidence, the claim that the umbilical cord should not be cut until one hour after birth is not supported by any recognized medical guideline or clinical study. Current consensus recommends a delay of 30 to 60 seconds, not one hour, and there is no indication that a shorter delay leaves the baby without enough blood. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

No further information is lacking to finalize this fact-check, as the evidence directly addresses the two core components of the claim: the requirement to sell plans and the requirement to cover the conditions.

The claim asserts that the plan guarantees both that insurers "must sell plans to any patient with preexisting conditions" **and** that the patient "will be covered in his plan." The evidence clearly supports the first part but explicitly refutes the second part, as the plan would allow insurers to exclude coverage for the preexisting conditions. Since the claim presents both parts as a combined guarantee, and the evidence refutes a substantial part of it, the claim is refuted.

`refuted`

claim: They [the Democrats] want to ... ban fracking.
justification: The claim is **REFUTED** because while some Democratic presidential primary candidates (e.g., [Sanders](https://www.npr.org/2020/02/11/804487306/proposals-to-ban-fracking-could-hurt-democrats-in-key-states), [Warren](https://www.denverpost.com/2019/09/10/democrats-fracking-bans-politics/)) and voter bases have supported a ban, the official party platform [stopped short of one](https://insideclimatenews.org/news/15072016/democratic-party-embrace-carbon-price-tax-hillary-clinton-bernie-sanders/), the 2020 nominee [explicitly rejected a ban](https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/31/politics/joe-biden-not-banning-fracking/index.html), and there is [no unified leadership policy or enacted executive ban](https://www.cnn.com/2019/09/16/politics/elizabeth-warren-bernie-sanders-ban-on-fracking-fact-check/index.html).
judge_reasoning:
Based on the evidence, the fact-check shows that while some prominent Democratic presidential primary candidates (e.g., Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren) have explicitly campaigned on banning fracking nationwide, the official Democratic Party platform has historically stopped short of calling for a complete ban. The 2020 presidential nominee, Joe Biden, explicitly stated he would not ban fracking, and there is no unified leadership policy supporting a federal ban. The evidence also highlights a key distinction between proposals targeting fracking on federal/public lands versus a nationwide ban affecting private property.

The evidence is sufficiently clear and comprehensive to render a decision, covering party platforms, presidential candidates, congressional actions, and state-level initiatives. No further investigation is required.

The claim that "They [the Democrats] want to ... ban fracking" implies a unified party-wide goal, which is not supported by the evidence. While some individual Democrats have advocated for bans, the party's official position and its recent presidential nominee have not supported a complete ban on fracking. Therefore, the claim is not accurate as a blanket statement. `refuted`
